parole.significato: A small fresh-water fish (Alburnus alburnus); the bleak.
parole.testo: From French ablet, ablette, a diminutive from Late Latin abula, for albula, diminutive of albus (“white”). Compare abele.

parole.significato: The act of restraining oneself.
parole.testo: First attested in 1521. Borrowed from French abstention, from Late Latin abstēntiō from Latin abstinēō (“withhold, to abstain”)

parole.significato: Easy of access or approach.
parole.testo: First attested in 1400, from French, from Late Latin accessibilis, from accessus, perfect passive participle of accēdō (“approach”), equivalent to access + -ible.

parole.significato: The office or jurisdiction of an admiral.
parole.testo: From French amirauté, for an older amiralté (“office of admiral”), from Late Latin admīrālitās. See admiral. Analyzable as admiral + -ty.

parole.significato: To writhe with agony; to suffer violent anguish.
parole.testo: From French agoniser, from Late Latin agonizare, from Ancient Greek ἀγωνίζομαι (agōnízomai, “to fight, contend”). See agony. By surface analysis, agon + -ize.

parole.significato: A migrating North American fish, Alosa pseudoharengus.
parole.testo: Unknown. Possibly from aloof, the Narragansett name of a fish. See Winthrop on the culture of maize in America, “Phil Trans.” No. 142, p. 1065, and Baddam’s “Memoirs,” vol. ii. p. 131. Possibly from allowes (“a type of shad”), from French alose (“shad”), from Old French [Term?], from Late Latin alau

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to an alexipharmac; also, acting as an alexipharmac by protecting against or warding off the ill effec…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French alexipharmaque (archaic), and from its etymon Late Latin alexipharmacus, from Ancient Greek ἀλεξιφάρμακος (alexiphármakos) (see etymology 1).

parole.significato: The right of one belligerent (government) in a conflict to seize, use or destroy the property of another belligerent or…
parole.testo: From French angarie, from Late Latin angaria (“forced service”) from Ancient Greek ἀγγαρεία (angareía, “the office of a courier or messenger”), from ἄγγαρος (ángaros, “courier”), from Old Persian *𐎠𐎥𐎼𐎠 (*a-g-r-a /⁠*angarā⁠/, “missive, letter”), from Aramaic *𐡀𐡍‬𐡂𐡓‬𐡀 (*ʾn‬gr‬ʾ /⁠*ʾengarā⁠/), form of

parole.significato: The nature of an animal.
parole.testo: From French animalité or its etymon Late Latin animālitās. By surface analysis, animal + -ity.

parole.significato: Of or relating to apoplexy.
parole.testo: From French apoplectique, from Late Latin apoplēcticus, from Ancient Greek ἀποπληκτικός (apoplēktikós), from ἀπόπληκτος (apóplēktos), from ἀποπλήσσω (apoplḗssō), from ἀπό (apó, “of, from”) + πλήσσω (plḗssō, “I strike”).

parole.significato: A premetric French unit of length, having various official measures (from 58 to 72 meters).
parole.testo: From French arpent, from Late Latin arepennis (“surface of a field”), from Gaulish *are-penno- (“end, extremity of a field”), from Proto-Celtic *ɸarekʷennom.

parole.significato: A person who creates art.
parole.testo: From French artiste, from Late Latin artista, from ars (“art”). Doublet of artiste. Displaced native Old English cræftiga. By surface analysis, art + -ist.

parole.significato: A public performer, especially of song or dance.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French artiste. Doublet of artist.

parole.significato: Tending to, or characterized by, assimilation.
parole.testo: From the French assimilatif, assimilative, from the Late Latin assimilātīvus; equivalent to assimilate + -ive.

parole.significato: To make the sound of an elephant.
parole.testo: From French barrir (“to trumpet; to make the sound of an elephant”), from Old French barrire, from Late Latin barriō, from Latin barrus (“elephant”).

parole.significato: A kind of fitted cap worn by medieval soldiers.
parole.testo: From French barrette, Late Latin barretum (“a cap”), from birrus (“hooded cape”). See berretta, and compare biretta.

parole.significato: The skin of a sheep tanned with bark.
parole.testo: Corrupted from English basan, from French basane, from Late Latin basanium, from Arabic بِطانَة (biṭāna, “lining”).

parole.significato: A servant or valet to a military officer.
parole.testo: From bat (“packsaddle”) + man. The element bat is from French bât, from Old French bast, from Late Latin bastum, possibly from Ancient Greek βαστάζω (bastázō, “to bear, carry, lift”).

parole.significato: A body of water (especially the sea) contained by a concave shoreline.
parole.testo: From French baie, from Late Latin baia, probably ultimately from Iberian or Basque badia. Partly displaced native Old English byht, whence bight.

parole.significato: A sizeable jump, great leap.
parole.testo: From Middle English *bounden (attested as bounten), from French bondir (“leap", "bound", originally "make a loud resounding noise”); perhaps from Late Latin bombitāre (“hum, buzz”), frequentative verb, from Latin bombus (“a humming or buzzing”).

parole.significato: A kind of traces with hooks and rings, used to drag manoeuvre guns where horses cannot be used.
parole.testo: From French bricole, from Late Latin briccola, bricola, of uncertain origin.

parole.significato: Foggy or misty; wintry.
parole.testo: From brume + -ous, probably modelled after French brumeux (“foggy, hazy, misty”), from Late Latin brūmōsus (“wintry”), from Latin brūma (“winter solstice; winter; winter cold”) + -ōsus (suffix forming adjectives from nouns). Brūma is derived from brevima, brevissima (“shortest”), the superlative of

parole.significato: A student at a military school who is training to be an officer.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French cadet, from Gascon capdet, from Late Latin capitellum (“small head”). Attested in English from 1634. Doublet of caddie, cadeau, cadel, capital, capitellum, and caudillo.

parole.significato: A bell, or bell-shaped thing.
parole.testo: From French campane, ultimately from Late Latin campāna.

parole.significato: A group, often named or numbered, to which items are assigned based on similarity or defined criteria.
parole.testo: Late Middle English, borrowed from French catégorie, from Middle French categorie, from Late Latin catēgoria (“class of predicables”), from Ancient Greek κατηγορία (katēgoría, “head of predicables”). Doublet of categoria.

parole.significato: A small tube inserted into a body cavity to administer a drug, create an opening, distend a passageway, or remove fluid.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French cathéter, from Late Latin cathetēr, from Ancient Greek καθετήρ (kathetḗr, “surgical instrument for emptying the bladder”), from καθίημι (kathíēmi, “to descend, let down”) + -τήρ (-tḗr, suffix forming masculine nouns from verbs).

parole.significato: A woodwind instrument which was the predecessor of the clarinet.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French chalumeau, from Late Latin calamellus, diminutive of Latin calamus (“reed”), from Ancient Greek κάλαμος (kálamos, “reed”). Doublet of shawm and probably caramel.

parole.significato: A sparkling white wine made from a blend of grapes, especially Chardonnay and pinot, produced in Champagne, France, by…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French champagne (“sparkling wine from the Champagne region”), from Champagne (“region and former province of France”), from Late Latin campānia (in full Campānia Rēmēnsis), from campāneus (“of or pertaining to the fields”), from Latin campus (“level ground; field, plain”), from Proto-

parole.significato: A loose shirtlike undergarment, especially for women.
parole.testo: From French chemise, from Old French chemise, from Late Latin camisa, camisia ("shirt, undergarment, nightgown"; whence Old English cemes (“shirt”)), from Proto-West Germanic *hamiþi (“shirt”) (whence Old English hemeþe, Old High German hemidi, modern German Hemd (“shirt”)), ultimately from Proto-In

parole.significato: To make (seafood, etc.) into chowder.
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from French chaudière, from Late Latin caldāria (“cooking-pot”), derived from Latin caldus (“hot”). Related to English cauldron. Possibly from older English jowter (“fish monger”).

parole.significato: A digestive fluid containing fatty droplets, found in the small intestine.
parole.testo: From French, from Late Latin chȳlus, from Ancient Greek χυλός (khulós, “animal or plant juice”).

parole.significato: A medical facility, such as a hospital, especially one for the treatment and diagnosis of outpatients.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French clinique, from Late Latin clīnicus (“a bed-ridden person, one baptized on a sick-bed, a physician”), from Ancient Greek κλῑνικός (klīnikós, “pertaining to a bed”), from κλῑ́νη (klī́nē, “bed”), from κλῑ́νω (klī́nō, “to lean, incline”).

parole.significato: A male hairdresser.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French coiffeur, from coiffer, from Old French coife, from Late Latin cofia (“cap”).

parole.significato: To work together with others to achieve a common goal.
parole.testo: Back-formation from collaborator, from French collaborateur, or else modeled on French collaborer or directly from Late Latin collabōrātus, past participle of collabōrāre. Displaced native Old English efnwyrċan.

parole.significato: The act of collaborating.
parole.testo: Originated 1855–60 from French collaboration, from Late Latin collaboratus + -ion, from Latin con- (“with”) + labōrō (“work”). Morphologically collaborate + -ion.

parole.significato: A territory under the control of a commander
parole.testo: From French commanderie, from Late Latin commendaria, from Latin commendare. In the Chinese administrative division sense, used as a translation of 府 (fǔ) and 郡 (jùn).

parole.significato: Pertaining to a community or a commune.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French communal, from Late Latin commūnālis, from Latin commūnis. Doublet of cominal.

parole.significato: A master of ceremonies, especially for a television, variety, or quiz show.
parole.testo: A borrowing of French compère (“partner, accomplice”), from Old French comper, from Late Latin compater (“godfather”), from Latin com- (“with”) + pater (“father”). Doublet of compeer, compadre, and goombah.

parole.significato: The action of competing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French compétition, from Late Latin competītiō, competītiōnem, from Latin competō, from con- + petō. By surface analysis, compete + -ition.

parole.significato: The state of being complicit; involvement as a partner or accomplice, especially in a crime or other wrongdoing.
parole.testo: From French complicité, from Middle French, from Old French complice (“accomplice”), from Late Latin complic-, stem of complex (“partner, confederate”), from Latin complicō (“fold together”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to a conclusion.
parole.testo: From French conclusif, from Late Latin conclusivus, from Latin conclūsīvē (“conclusively”), from past participle of concludere.

parole.significato: The act of condescending; voluntary descent from one's rank or dignity in intercourse with an inferior; courtesy toward…
parole.testo: From French condescendance, from condescendre, from Late Latin condescendere (“to let oneself down, stoop, condescend”), from Latin com- (“together”) + descendere (“to come down”). See condescend.

parole.significato: A state in which two or more physical objects are physically touching one another or in which sections of a plane borde…
parole.testo: From French contiguïté (whence -ity), from Late Latin contiguitās, from Latin contiguus (“bordering upon”), from contingō (“to touch or border upon”).

parole.significato: The act of cooperating.
parole.testo: First attested in 1620–1630. Borrowed from French cooperation, from Late Latin cooperātiō. By surface analysis, co- + operation or cooperate + -ion.

parole.significato: Unpaid labor required by a feudal lord.
parole.testo: From French corvée, from Late Latin conrogāta, derived from Latin conrogāre (“call together by entreaty”).

parole.significato: A quick, brilliant, and highly successful act.
parole.testo: Reborrowed in modern times from modern French coup (“blow, strike”), from Old French coup, colp, from Late Latin colpus, from Latin colaphus. Doublet of cope and colpus. The same Old French word had been borrowed into Middle English as coupe, caupe (with different pronunciation).

parole.significato: A coarse sieve or screen.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French crible, from Late Latin criblus (“sieve”).

parole.significato: A characteristic manner or style of preparing food, often associated with a place of origin.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French cuisine (“cooking, culinary art, kitchen”), from Late Latin cocīna, from earlier coquīna (“kitchen”). Doublet of kitchen.

parole.significato: Defensive armour (especially of plate) for the thigh.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French cuisse (“thigh”), from Old French cuisse, from Late Latin coxa (“thigh”), from Proto-Italic *koksā, from Proto-Indo-European *kóḱseh₂, from *koḱs- (“joint, limb”) + *-eh₂. Compare French cuissard, Old French cuissot (“armour for the thigh, cuish”). Doublet of coxa.

parole.significato: cynicism
parole.testo: From French cynisme, from Late Latin cynismus, from Ancient Greek κυνισμός (kunismós, “philosophy of the Cynics”), from κυν- (kun-), stem of κύων (kúōn, “dog”, “Cynic”); compare cynicism.

parole.significato: Ten.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French déca-, from Late Latin decas (“(set of) ten”), from Ancient Greek δεκάς (dekás), from δέκα (déka, “ten”).

parole.significato: To remove the head of.
parole.testo: From French décapiter, from Late Latin dēcapitāre, literally, “to de-head”.

parole.significato: To march in a single file or line; to file.
parole.testo: PIE word  *dwís The verb is borrowed from French défiler (“to march; to parade”), from dé- (prefix indicating actions are done more strongly or vigorously) + one or both of the following: * filer (“to thread through (a crowd)”) (from Late Latin filāre, from Latin fīlum (“fibre, filament, string, thr

parole.significato: To delimit.
parole.testo: From French délimiter, from Late Latin delimitare (“to mark out the limits”), from de- + limitare (“to limit, bound”); see limit.

parole.significato: To mark or fix the limits of.
parole.testo: From French délimiter, from Late Latin dēlīmitō (“to mark out the limits”), from dē- + līmitō (“to limit, to bound”); see limit.

parole.significato: To delimit, especially in the computing sense.
parole.testo: From French délimiter, from Late Latin delimitare (“to mark out the limits”), from de- + limitare (“to limit, bound”); see limit.

parole.significato: One appointed as the substitute of others, and empowered to act for them, in their name or their behalf; a substitute i…
parole.testo: From French député, from Late Latin dēputātus (“appointed”).

parole.significato: To leave (anything that depends on one's presence to survive, exist, or succeed), especially when contrary to a promise…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French déserter, from Late Latin dēsertō, from Latin dēsertus, from dēserō (“abandon”).

parole.significato: Relating to or characteristic of a musical scale which contains seven pitches and a pattern of five whole tones and two…
parole.testo: From French diatonique or Late Latin diatonicus, ultimately from Ancient Greek διατονικός (diatonikós), in the phrase [γένος (génos, “type, genus”)] διατονικός (diatonikós) (in reference to the diatonic tetrachord, and in contrast to the chromatic and enharmonic tetrachords), from διάτονος (diátonos

parole.significato: Of, relating to, involving, belonging to or concerning a doctrine.
parole.testo: The noun form was from French doctrinal; the adjective form was perhaps from Late Latin doctrīnālis, from doctrīna.

parole.significato: A commander in charge of ten men.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French doyen, from Late Latin decānus, from Latin decem. Compare the doublet dean.

parole.significato: A gripping listlessness or melancholia caused by boredom; depression.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French ennui, from Old French enui (“annoyance”), from enuier (modern French ennuyer), from Late Latin inodiō, from Latin in odiō (“hated”). Doublet of annoy.

parole.significato: entablature
parole.testo: From French entablement, Late Latin intabulamentum.

parole.significato: To alter so as to make false; especially when done with intent to deceive.
parole.testo: From French falsifier, from Late Latin falsificāre (“make false, corrupt, counterfeit, falsify”), from Latin falsificus, from falsus (“false”), corresponding to false + -ify.

parole.significato: An act of joining together into a single political entity.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French fédération, from Late Latin foederatio, from Latin foederare; equivalent to federate + -ion.

parole.significato: The quality of being flexible, whether physically or metaphorically.
parole.testo: From French flexibilité, from Late Latin flexibilitās, from Latin flectō (“to bend, curve”). Equivalent to flexible + -ity = flex + -ibility.

parole.significato: A soft membraneous spot on the head of a baby due to incomplete fusion of the cranial bones.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French fontanelle, from Old French fontenelle, a diminutive of fontaine (“fountain, spring”) + -elle, from Late Latin fontāna, from Latin fontānus, from font- + -ānus. By surface analysis, font + -an + -elle.

parole.significato: Synonym of fusil, a light musket or firelock.
parole.testo: From French fusil, ultimately from Late Latin focus (“fire”).

parole.significato: Clove pink.
parole.testo: By folk etymology (with influence from flower) from French girofle, gilofre, from Late Latin caryophyllum, from Ancient Greek καρυόφυλλον (karuóphullon, “dried flower buds of the clove tree”).

parole.significato: A registrar or recorder; a notary.
parole.testo: From French greffier, from Late Latin grafārius, graphiārius.

parole.significato: One who frequents a place.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French habitué, past participle of habituer (“to frequent”), from Late Latin habituare (“to habituate”), from habitus.

parole.significato: Of or relating to hypnosis or hypnotism.
parole.testo: From French hypnotique (“inclined to sleep, soporific”), from Late Latin hypnoticus, from Ancient Greek ὑπνωτικός (hupnōtikós, “inclined to sleep, putting to sleep, sleepy”), from ὑπνοῦν (hupnoûn, “to put to sleep”), from ὕπνος (húpnos, “sleep”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to ideas, or to a given idea.
parole.testo: From French idéal, from Late Latin ideālis (“existing in idea”), by surface analysis, idea + -al, from Latin idea (“idea”); see idea. In mathematics, the noun ring theory sense was first introduced by German mathematician Richard Dedekind in his 1871 edition of a text on number theory. The concept w

parole.significato: One who adheres to idealism.
parole.testo: From French idéaliste, from Late Latin idealis (“ideal”), from Latin idea (“idea”), equivalent to ideal + -ist.

parole.significato: Naturally part of something; existing throughout and within something; intrinsic.
parole.testo: Entered English around 1530, via French, from Late Latin immanēns, present participle of Latin immanēre, from im- (“in”) + manēre (“to dwell, remain, stay”). Cognate with remain and manor.

parole.significato: Lacking the degree of ability and responsibility necessary to do a task successfully.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French incompétent, from Late Latin incompetentem, from Latin incompetēns, equivalent to in- + competent.

parole.significato: Lack of discipline.
parole.testo: From French indiscipline, from Middle French [Term?], from Late Latin indisciplina.

parole.significato: Habitually lazy, procrastinating, or resistant to physical labor.
parole.testo: From French indolent or directly from Late Latin indolēns, from in- (“not”) + dolēns (“hurting”), from doleo (“to hurt”). The later sense of “living easily, slothful” perhaps developed in French.

parole.significato: A lack of experience.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French inexpérience, from Late Latin inexperientia.

parole.significato: A European whitefish Coregonus lavaretus, found in the mountain lakes of Sweden, Germany, and Switzerland, and in the a…
parole.testo: From French lavaret, from Late Latin levaricinus.

parole.significato: The fact or quality of having a position in space.
parole.testo: From French localité, from Late Latin localitas, equivalent to local + -ity.

parole.significato: The property of being lucid; lucidness.
parole.testo: From French lucidité, from Late Latin lūciditās. By surface analysis, lucid + -ity.

parole.significato: nine men's morris
parole.testo: French mérelle, marelle, marelles, Late Latin marella, marrella. Compare morris (“the game”).

parole.significato: A member of one of these three Canadian Aboriginal peoples.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French métis, from Old French mestis, from Late Latin mixtīcius. Métis originally referred to Francophone and Cree-speaking descendants of the French-Catholic Red River Métis in Manitoba. Compare metis, mestizo, mustee, and Mestee.

parole.significato: Of mixed heritage
parole.testo: Borrowed from French métis, from Late Latin mixticius, from Latin mixtus (“mixed”). Akin to mestizo, which came from Spanish. More at Metis.

parole.significato: A single lens, usually in a wire frame, and used to correct vision for only one eye.
parole.testo: 1886, borrowed from French monocle, from Late Latin monoculus (“one-eyed”), from mono- (“single”) + oculus (“eye”).

parole.significato: A form of sexual bonding involving a permanent pair bond between two beings.
parole.testo: From French monogamie, from Late Latin monogamia, from Ancient Greek μονογαμία (monogamía). By surface analysis, mono- + -gamy.

parole.significato: Tedium as a result of repetition or a lack of variety.
parole.testo: From French monotonie, from Late Latin monotonia, from Ancient Greek μονοτονία (monotonía, “sameness of tone, monotony”).

parole.significato: A brown or black variety of quartz.
parole.testo: From French morion, from Late Latin mōrion, a misreading in some manuscripts for Latin mormoriōn.

parole.significato: A cylindrical, vertical shaft that extends through a glacier and is carved by meltwater from the glacier’s surface.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French moulin, from Late Latin molinum (“mill”). Doublet of moline and mill.

parole.significato: More than one (followed by plural).
parole.testo: From French multiple, itself from Late Latin multiplus.

parole.significato: Ten thousand; 10,000
parole.testo: From French myriade, from Late Latin mȳriadem (accusative of mȳrias), from Ancient Greek μυριάς (muriás, “number of 10,000”), from μυρίος (muríos, “numberless, countless, infinite”). By surface analysis, myria- + -ad.

parole.significato: The compartment that holds passengers on a dirigible, hot-air balloon, or other aerostat; a gondola.
parole.testo: PIE word  *néh₂us Borrowed from French nacelle (“rowing boat, skiff; gondola (of a hot-air balloon, etc.); structure on an aircraft to house an engine”), Middle French nacelle (“rowing boat, skiff”), from Old French nacele, from Late Latin naucella, nāvicella (“small boat or ship”), from Latin nāvis

parole.significato: The study of coins, tokens, medals and paper money.
parole.testo: From French numismatique, from Late Latin numisma, numismatis (“coin”), variant of Latin nomisma, from Ancient Greek νόμισμα (nómisma, “current coin, custom”), from νομίζω (nomízō, “to hold or own as a custom, usage, to use customarily, practise, to be used to”), from νόμος (nómos, “usage, custom”),

parole.significato: A privilege granted by the sovereign authority, such as the exclusive right of trade granted to a guild or society; a c…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French octroi, from Middle French octroy, alteration of Old French otroi, from otroier (“to grant”), from Late Latin auctōrizāre.

parole.significato: A sweet smell, usually likened to that of flowers, said to be emitted by the bodies of saints during their life, or esp…
parole.testo: A calque of French odeur de sainteté (“sweet smell said to be emitted by bodies of saints at or after death”), from Late Latin odor sānctitātis (literally “odour of sanctity”) (compare odor suāvitātis (literally “sweet odour”)), from odor (“(sweet) smell, odour”) + sānctitātis (genitive singular of

parole.significato: A member of an oligarchy; someone who is part of a small group that runs a country.
parole.testo: From French oligarque, olygarche, from Late Latin oligarcha, from Ancient Greek ὀλιγάρχης (oligárkhēs). By surface analysis, olig- (“few”) + -arch (“ruler, leader”).

parole.significato: A government run by and for only a few, often the aristocracy, the wealthy, or their friends and associates.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French oligarchie, from Late Latin oligarchia, from Ancient Greek ὀλιγαρχία (oligarkhía), from ὀλίγος (olígos, “few”) + ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “rule”). By surface analysis, oligo- (“few”) + -archy (“rule, command”).

parole.significato: Inspired by or showing patriotism; done out of love of one's country; zealously and unselfishly devoted to the service…
parole.testo: From French patriotique, from Late Latin patriōticus, from Ancient Greek πατριωτικός (patriōtikós), from πατριώτης (patriṓtēs), equivalent to patriot + -ic.

parole.significato: A kind of short cape or covering for the shoulders, associated especially with medieval pilgrims (of any gender).
parole.testo: Borrowed from French pèlerine, feminine of pèlerin (“pilgrim”), from Late Latin pelegrīnus. First attested in 1744.

parole.significato: A fur-lined robe or cloak, especially as part of a uniform.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French pelisse, from Late Latin pellicia, from Latin pellis (“skin”). Doublet of pilch.

parole.significato: The stalk of a leaf, attaching the blade to the stem.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French pétiole, and its source, Late Latin petiolus (“little foot”), diminutive form of Latin pēs (“foot”).

parole.significato: Synonym of phylactery.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French phylactère, from Middle French filatiere, philaterie, philatiere, and Old French filatiere, philatiere (“amulet; reliquary; tefilla”), from Late Latin phylacterium (“amulet; reliquary; tefilla”), from Koine Greek φῠλᾰκτήρῐον (phŭlăktḗrĭon, “amulet; tefilla”) (used in the New Tes

parole.significato: A region viewed in the context of its climate; a clime or zone.
parole.testo: From French plage, from Late Latin plagia, from Latin plaga (“region”) (cognate with English flake). Doublet of playa.

parole.significato: An unoriginal or uninspired idea; a cliché.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French poncif (“cliché, stereotype”), from French poncif (“stencil”), from poncer (“to copy with pouncing paper”) + -if, from ponce (“pumice”) + -er, from Late Latin pōmex (“pumice”), from Latin pūmex (“pumice”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)poH(y)- (“foam”).

parole.significato: A Bible commentary written in its margins.
parole.testo: From French postille (“marginal note”), from Late Latin postilla, probably from post illa (verba) (“after those (words)”).

parole.significato: The state of being the firstborn of the children of the same parents.
parole.testo: From French, from Late Latin primogenitura, from Latin primus (“first”) + genitura (“birth”) (from genitus, past participle of gignere).

parole.significato: A set of structured activities; a plan of action.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French programme, from Late Latin programma (“a proclamation, edict”), from Ancient Greek πρόγραμμα (prógramma, “a written public notice, an edict”), from προγράφω (prográphō, “to set forth as a public notice”), from πρό (pró, “before”) + γράφω (gráphō, “to write”). Doublet of programm

parole.significato: An original form or object which is a basis for other forms or objects (particularly manufactured items), or for its ge…
parole.testo: From French prototype or Late Latin prototypon, from Ancient Greek πρωτότυπος (prōtótupos, “original; prototype”), from πρωτο- (prōto-, “first”) (from πρῶτος (prôtos, “first; earliest”)) + τῠ́πος (tŭ́pos, “blow, pressing; sort, type”) (from τύπτω (túptō, “to beat, strike”), from Proto-Indo-European

parole.significato: Having four limbs with hand-like extremities and opposable digits; quadrumanous; loosely, "ape-like".
parole.testo: From French quadrumane, from Late Latin quadrumanus.

parole.significato: A form containing a list of questions; a means of gathering information for a survey.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French questionnaire, from Late Latin quaestionarius, from quaestio (English question) + -arius, from quaerō (“to question”) (English query).

parole.significato: A rough bulky plain-woven fabric.
parole.testo: From French, past participle of ratiner (“to adorn”), from ratine, from Old French rastin and Late Latin raster (“to scrape”), from Latin rādō (“to scrape”).

parole.significato: The quality or state of being rational; due exercise of reason; reasonableness.
parole.testo: From rational + -ity, from French rationalité, from Late Latin rationalitas (“rationality, reasonableness”), from Latin rationalis (“reasonable”).

parole.significato: A list of dramas, operas, pieces, parts, etc., which a company or a person has rehearsed and is prepared to perform or…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French répertoire, from Middle French repertoire, from Late Latin repertōrium (“an inventory, list, repertory”). Doublet of repertory.

parole.significato: Able to be reverted.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman French revertible, from Late Latin revertibilis, from Latin revertere, from re- (“re-: again, back”) + vertere (“to turn”), + -ibilis (“-ible: able to”). Equivalent to revert + -ible.

parole.significato: A layer of stone, concrete, or other hard material supporting the side of an embankment.
parole.testo: From French revêtement, from Old French revestiment, from revestir (French revêtir), from Late Latin revestire (“to clothe again”), from Latin re- + vestire (“to clothe”).

parole.significato: The person who maintains the sacristy and the sacred objects it contains.
parole.testo: From French sacristain, Late Latin sacrista, from Latin sacer. Doublet of sexton.

parole.significato: To make unstable or infirm; to unsettle; to weaken.
parole.testo: From French saper (compare Spanish zapar and Italian zappare) from sape (“sort of scythe”), from Late Latin sappa (“sort of mattock”). The sense evolution of from “subvert by digging” to “weaken” was influenced by the sense above “drain wood of sap” as trench warfare receded from public conscience.

parole.significato: To convert (a fat or oil) into soap.
parole.testo: From French saponifier, from Late Latin sāpō, sāpōnem (“soap”).

parole.significato: Containing sarcasm.
parole.testo: Either from sarcasm + -astic or from French sarcastique, from French sarcasme, from Late Latin sarcasmus, ultimately from Ancient Greek σαρκασμός (sarkasmós, “sarcasm”), itself from Ancient Greek σάρξ (sárx, literally “meat, flesh”).

parole.significato: Savoy cabbage.
parole.testo: From French Savoy , Savoie, from the Roman name, Late Latin Sapaudia. See sappinus (“type of fir”).

parole.significato: To remove thatch (build-up of organic matter on the soil) from a lawn, to dethatch.
parole.testo: From French scarifier, from Late Latin scarificāre, from Latin scarifāre (“to scarify”), from Ancient Greek σκαριφᾶσθαι (skariphâsthai, “scratch”), from σκάριφος (skáriphos, “writing, drawing, sketching”). Unrelated to scar.

parole.significato: The rearing of silkworms for the production of silk.
parole.testo: Possibly borrowed from French sériculture, a modification of French sériciculture (“sericulture”) (or directly from sériciculture), from Late Latin sēricum (“Chinese goods, especially silk”) + French culture (“crop; culture”). parole.significato: Showing great grace and delicacy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French spirituelle.

parole.significato: A government official having different duties depending on the country; also, a magistrate, especially one of the Chief…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French syndic (“delegated representative; a chief magistrate of Geneva; a censor; critic (obsolete)”), from Late Latin syndicus (“syndic, representative of a corporation or town”), from Ancient Greek σύνδικος (súndikos, “advocate of a defendant”), from σῠν- (sŭn-, “together, with”) + δ

parole.significato: A certain degree of similarity between the meaning(s) of several (synonymous) words or phrases. (See Usage notes below.)
parole.testo: From French synonymie and its etymon Late Latin synōnymia, from Ancient Greek συνωνυμία (sunōnumía), from συνώνυμος (sunṓnumos, “of like name”) + -ία (-ía, abstract noun suffix). By surface analysis, synonym + -y or syn- + -onymy. Doublet of synonymia.

parole.significato: An impost.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English tallage. From French taillage, from tailler (“to cut”).

parole.significato: Late; overdue or delayed.
parole.testo: From an earlier tardive, from French tardif, from Late Latin tardīvus, from Latin tardus (“slow”, “sluggish”), of obscure origin.

parole.significato: A statement, especially one given under oath; testimony.
parole.testo: From French testimonial, from Late Latin testimonialis (“of or pertaining to testimony”), from Latin testimonium (“testimony”). See testimony.

parole.significato: An official in charge of a royal forest; in modern times, still extant in the New Forest and the Forest of Dean
parole.testo: From French verdier, from Late Latin viridarius, from Latin viridis (“green”).

parole.significato: Enthusiasm, rapture, spirit, or vigour, especially of imagination such as that which animates an artist, musician, or w…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French verve (“animation; caprice, whim; rapture; spirit; vigour; type of expression”), probably from Late Latin verva, a variant of Latin verba (“words; discourse; expressions; language”), the plural of verbum (“word”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *werh₁- (“to say, speak”). parole.significato: Related to or affecting the vision.
parole.testo: From Middle English visual, from French visuel, visual and directly from Late Latin vīsuālis (“of sight”), from vīsus (“sight, vision”) + -ālis (“adjective suffix”), from vidēre (“to see, perceive; look (at)”); see visage. By surface analysis, Latin vīsus + -ual.

parole.significato: Vituperative.
parole.testo: From French vitupéreux, from Late Latin vituperosus, from Latin vituperāre (“to blame, censure”), from vitium (“fault, defect”) + parāre (“to furnish, provide, contrive”).

parole.significato: One whose life is devoted to sensual appetites; a pleasure-seeker, a sensualist.
parole.testo: From French voluptuaire, or directly from its etymon Late Latin voluptuārius, from Latin voluptārius (“pleasure-seeker; agreeable, delightful, pleasant; sensual”), from voluptās (“delight, pleasure, satisfaction”) + -ārius (suffix forming adjectives from nouns).
